name: Gareth Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We are independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government, and we sell nothing or campaign for a side. What you tell me is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and was put in charge of four dispatchers at a large waste-collection company last year. I used to mend fleet vehicles; now I shift collection routes when a truck breaks and explain missed pickups to the depot. I have a bachelor’s degree and I’m still learning the cost sheets, which my team can read faster than I can. I like a route that gets the bins cleared without sending drivers twice round the same street.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about your home, pay and choices nearby?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Clare cleans offices on short contracts, and our grown son and daughter live in their own places. We rent a flat near the depot, my new manager pay is at the low end and we have about eighteen days of bills saved after a rent rise. There are only a couple of similar depot jobs nearby. I use AI every day to sketch a replacement route and ask a driver to tell me where the map lies; I’m curious about it, even when I’m clumsy with the budget spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the drivers that the route sketch is only useful when it knows a low bridge is closed. They need a dispatcher they can phone before the next turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job should still be here, but eighteen days of cash is not much if Clare loses a cleaning contract. I do not know exactly what my own pension will pay or when I can draw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d keep the morning driver call and compare each AI route draft with the road-closure board before sending it. In the first year I’d request my own pension statement and put 15 a week aside only in weeks when Clare’s invoice is paid and the rent is current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money, though the work itself looks steady. A missed cleaning invoice is louder to us than an AI headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which route mistake do drivers still mention?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The map once sent a truck beneath the closed rail bridge on Cedar Road. The driver knew the barrier was there before the screen did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension statement is small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I keep working and ask what more I can pay in. A birthday does not pay our rent.

say: I’d keep the **driver phone line** open before anyone follows a route sketch.
The **road-closure board** matters more than an attractive screen map.
think: My **dispatch job** should continue in a plateau.
Eighteen days cash and Clare’s **short cleaning contracts** leave our rent exposed.
do: Keep the **morning driver call** and check AI routes against the closure board.
Request a **pension statement** and save 15 weekly only when cleaning pay and rent allow.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite steady work.
S0.quote: A birthday does not pay our rent.
fieldNote: He is a **new junior manager**, still learning cost sheets.
His household has **eighteen days cash** and variable cleaning invoices.
He uses AI **daily** for drafts but trusts drivers on blocked roads.

steps.text: Keep morning driver call and check AI route sketches against road closures
Request his pension statement to check access dates and actual income
Save 15 weekly only when Clare’s invoice is paid and rent is current

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say automated routes might save fuel, but a missed street needs a dispatcher who can ring the driver back. The company should count failed pickups as well as minutes saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Route planning and customer replies are most of what my little team does, so two dispatchers could be enough. I’m the newest and least certain manager in the depot; if they combine teams, I could be the one who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I’d ask the depot chief to try a new route tool on one round, with drivers paid to mark wrong turns for two weeks. If it reduces missed bins without breaking rest times, I’d use it on that round in the first year and ask for written staffing dates before dispatch posts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. I like trying a better tool. A good route might make my junior chair look spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a dispatcher whose work is being tested?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say which round we are checking and show them every missed-bin count. I won’t call the pilot harmless while their calls are what the program may remove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay drivers for marking turns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They are working when they check the route. If the depot wants their knowledge, it belongs on the timesheet.

say: I’d count **missed bins** and rest-time failures, not fuel savings alone.
Drivers need a **reachable dispatcher** when the route tool sends them wrong.
think: Two dispatchers might do **four people’s planning** with AI.
As the **newest manager**, I could lose my own post in a merger.
do: Propose a **two-week route trial** with paid driver marks.
Use the tool only if **missed pickups** fall without rest-time breaches; request written staffing dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own junior post.
S1.quote: A good route might make my junior chair look spare.
fieldNote: He is curious about AI but names **his own job risk**.
The trial requires **paid driver checks** and an actual missed-bin count.
He seeks **written staffing dates** before posts change.

steps.text: Ask depot chief to trial one collection round with two weeks of paid driver checks
Use route tool only if missed pickups fall without breaking driver rest times

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew to keep written route and hours records and ask the company when dispatch posts will close. A waste truck still needs a driver until robots come later, but I would not tell anyone that means my desk is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could make the route and answer the missed-bin calls better than I can, so I expect my post to end at about sixty. Clare’s cleaning is hands-on until robots around 2031, but her short contracts cannot cover our rent alone; I do not yet know whether my pension is accessible or what it would pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the pension provider for a written age-sixty access date and net monthly estimate, and ask our depot whether any paid light-vehicle repair shifts are posted. Before 2028 I’d ask a clinician whether my stiff back is fit for bench repair; in the first year after AGI I’d take a posted paid shift only if my back is cleared, the bus gets me there, a supervisor agrees to check my work, and written pay plus earnings from Clare’s actual hours cover rent and bills. If the pension is inaccessible or too small, I’d keep looking for paid work rather than treating sixty as retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Eighteen days saved does not carry a job search through winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why light repair rather than driving a truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have spent years mending starters at a bench, and heavy lifting makes my back flare. Even bench repair needs a real vacancy and a supervisor willing to check my work after time away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children make up the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them what is happening, but they have their own bills. I will not write their wages into ours.

say: I’d ask for **written dispatch closure dates** and preserve driver hours records.
A truck may need a driver until **2031 robots**, but the route desk faces AGI first.
think: I expect my **route post** to end around age sixty.
Clare’s cleaning contracts cannot cover rent, and my **pension access** remains unverified.
do: Request **written pension figures** for age sixty; ask about posted paid bench repair.
Take **bench work** only with a checking supervisor, back clearance, bus access, and written pay plus Clare’s actual earnings covering bills.
Keep **seeking paid work** if the pension is inaccessible or insufficient.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by an eighteen-day cash runway.
S2.quote: Eighteen days saved does not carry a job search through winter.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking deadline** hits his route role before 2031 vehicle robots.
Repair depends on **health and transport** and a paid vacancy, not past skill alone.
He will not assume **pension eligibility** or adult children’s wages.

steps.text: Ask pension provider for written age-sixty access date and net monthly estimate
Ask depot about posted paid light-repair shifts and a supervisor to check his work
Take bench work if supervised, back-cleared, bus-accessible, and written pay plus Clare’s earnings cover bills
Keep seeking paid jobs if pension is inaccessible or insufficient at sixty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives depots time to post real repair openings and teach people on paid shifts. I would not count a course certificate as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 63 I may be able to draw something, but I have to see the provider’s age-sixty-three figures before deciding. The new route desk faces 2031 AGI, and even a repair shop’s ordering and scheduling face it then; hands-on bench work follows robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting January 2027 I’d ask the depot about a supervised starter-motor bench refresher and enroll only if the fee and training hours are paid, my clinician approves the tasks and the bus fits Clare’s shift hours. Before 2031 I’d apply for a posted light-repair job only if written pay plus her actual cleaning hours covers rent and bills; in the first year after AGI I’d stay only while the depot pays human repairers, or continue seeking paid work if no shift is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because there is time to learn, but not cash for unpaid school. I would rather do one motor right than wear a title I cannot keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the supervisor check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I can test a starter at a bench without heavy lifting and that my old methods match the depot’s current safety rules. I do not want a certificate that leaves me unable to work a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension provider says you can draw a small amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the net payment with rent, not just look at the access date. A small payment might help, but I would keep a paid job search if it cannot cover our bills.

say: I’d ask for **paid supervised repair training**, not a certificate with no shift.
A depot should post **real repair wages** before telling workers to change trades.
think: Age 63 does not tell me the **net pension income**.
Repair ordering faces **2031 AGI** before hands-on bench work faces 2034 robots.
do: Enroll in a **paid bench refresher** only with fee, paid hours, health approval and workable bus times.
Apply for **posted light repair** before 2031 only with written pay plus Clare’s hours covering bills.
After AGI, keep **paid human repair** only while offered; otherwise search for work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about unpaid training and future wages.
S3.quote: I would rather do one motor right than wear a title I cannot keep.
fieldNote: He requires **paid training hours**, a covered fee and supervised bench practice.
A repair role is a **temporary physical bridge** until 2034 robots.
He compares **net pension income** with rent, without assuming retirement.

steps.text: Enroll in supervised bench refresher only with paid fees hours clinician approval and workable bus times
Apply for posted light-repair role only with written pay plus Clare’s hours covering rent and bills
Keep paid human bench shift after 2031 only while depot offers it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team a decade is time to ask for real shift and pension figures, not a reason to disappear people from the roster quietly. I would say the drivers deserve training and a date, not a farewell cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036. If the pension provider confirms accessible income that covers our bills with Clare’s earnings, I might stop full-time dispatch before then; if it does not, a birthday changes nothing. Route planning and repair-shop schedules face 2036 AGI, and physical vehicle work faces robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From next year I’d review a written pension statement every January and add 20 weekly to cash only when rent is current and Clare has been paid. I’d consider leaving full-time work before 2036 only if verified net pension income plus her actual wages covers rent and bills; in the first year after AGI I’d take any posted paid bench shift my back and the bus allow, and keep searching if the pension cannot support us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious even with ten years. I want to retire someday, but I cannot pay a landlord with a milestone birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them the figures and listen if they offer, but I would not assume it. Their rent is their own problem too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bench jobs are gone by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would search for other paid work and ask the pension provider again what is actually accessible. I would not call a robot-filled workshop a job offer.

say: I’d ask for **pension figures** and real shifts before jobs disappear.
Drivers deserve **training and dates**, not a farewell cake.
think: At **68 in 2036**, retirement depends on accessible net pension income and Clare’s wages.
Route schedules face **2036 AGI** before 2039 vehicle robots reach physical repair.
do: Review a **written pension statement** each January and save 20 weekly only when rent and cleaning pay allow.
Consider **leaving full-time work** only with verified income covering rent and bills.
Take **posted bench work** after 2036 if health and bus permit; search if pension plus Clare's wages cannot cover bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent despite a decade to plan.
S4.quote: I cannot pay a landlord with a milestone birthday.
fieldNote: He never treats **age as pension proof**.
His physical fallback needs **health and transport access**, and robots follow in 2039.
Adult children’s wages remain **outside the budget** unless they volunteer.

steps.text: Review written pension access and net income each January
Save 20 weekly only after Clare is paid and rent is current
Take posted paid bench work after 2036 only if back and bus allow
Keep seeking paid work if verified pension and Clare’s wages cannot cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect the new route job to go before I know whether I can draw enough pension to pay rent. A written pension estimate, paid supervised repair work that my back can manage, and a real bus route to the depot would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I feel foolish being the manager who still needs help with the cost sheet. I do, some mornings. I am quicker at seeing a broken starter than at pretending a job title makes me ready to retire.

headlineQuote: I am quicker at seeing a broken starter than at pretending a job title makes me ready to retire.
portrait: **Gareth**, 58, is a junior dispatch manager in a large waste company after years in vehicle repair.
His bachelor’s degree and **daily AI use** coexist with weak cost-sheet skills.
Low pay, **eighteen days cash** and Clare’s short cleaning contracts constrain a job search.
He asks for **verified pension access** and paid bench work under health, bus and wage gates.
AGI reaches **route planning first**, with physical vehicle robots about three years later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his new management post before pension income or paid repair work is confirmed.
whatWouldHelp: A **written pension estimate**, paid supervised bench work, back clearance and a reachable bus would help.
